content: Many perimenopausal and early postmenopausal women experience menopausal symptoms, with hot flushes being the most common. These symptoms are caused by fluctuating estrogen levels and can often be alleviated by hormone therapy (HT). However, due to concerns about the risks and benefits of HT, its global use has significantly declined. As a result, many women are seeking alternative treatments. Given the large number of women opting not to use HT, it is increasingly important to identify evidence-based lifestyle modifications, such as exercise, that may help reduce vasomotor menopausal symptoms. The objective of this review was to evaluate the effectiveness of various exercise interventions in managing vasomotor symptoms, such as hot flushes and night sweats, in symptomatic perimenopausal and postmenopausal women. To achieve this, randomized controlled trials (RCTs) were identified through searches of multiple electronic bibliographic databases, including the Cochrane Menstrual Disorders and Subfertility Group Specialised Trials Register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, EMBASE, PsycINFO, the Science Citation Index, the Social Science Citation Index, CINAHL, and SPORTDiscus. The search included studies published up to March 3, 2014. The selection criteria included RCTs that compared any type of exercise intervention with no treatment, a control group, or other treatments for managing vasomotor symptoms in symptomatic perimenopausal or postmenopausal women. Five studies met the inclusion criteria. Two review authors independently selected the studies, and three review authors independently extracted the data. The primary outcome of interest was vasomotor symptoms, specifically hot flushes and night sweats. Data were combined to calculate standardized mean differences (SMDs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs), and statistical heterogeneity was assessed using the I² statistic. The overall quality of the evidence was evaluated using the GRADE methodology. The review included five RCTs involving a total of 733 women. These studies compared exercise with no active treatment, exercise with yoga, and exercise with HT. The quality of the evidence was low due to limitations in study design, inconsistency, and imprecision. When comparing exercise with no active treatment (three studies, 454 women), there was no evidence of a difference between the groups in the frequency or intensity of vasomotor symptoms (SMD -0.10, 95% CI -0.33 to 0.13, I² = 30%, low-quality evidence). Similarly, when comparing exercise with yoga (two studies, 279 women), no evidence of a difference in symptom frequency or intensity was found (SMD -0.03, 95% CI -0.45 to 0.38, I² = 61%, low-quality evidence). One trial, which could not be included in the meta-analyses, compared three groups: exercise plus soy milk, soy milk only, and a control group. This trial suggested that exercise was more effective than the comparators, but the sample size was small. In one trial comparing exercise with HT, the HT group reported significantly fewer hot flushes over 24 hours than the exercise group (mean difference 5.8, 95% CI 3.17 to 8.43, 14 participants). None of the trials reported evidence of differences between groups in terms of adverse effects, but the data on adverse effects were very limited. In conclusion, the evidence was insufficient to determine whether exercise is an effective treatment for vasomotor menopausal symptoms. One small study suggested that HT is more effective than exercise. There was also insufficient evidence to determine the relative effectiveness of exercise compared with HT or yoga.
